I ran a mini campaign (3.5) were the players we a pack of goblins. Their homeland was being deforested an encroached on by an expanding humanoid settlement. Like all good settlements the farmers were in semi-fortified houses, and the nearby town provided regular patrols.

Set-up

The players had to complete a handful of objectives.

  1. Secure slaves (humanoids or otherwise),

  2. Secure tools and supplies (from farms or the town),

  3. Scout a new home (6 options give or take),

  4. Clear the selected home, &

  5. Move the elderly and children goblins.

To make the campaign go faster I premade a about 30 level 2 goblins. All the goblins had at least one level of barbarian, cleric, rogue, or sorcerer. This class determined to some extent their feats. Those with sorcerer at level 1 had increased spell damage at the expense of having to shout whenever casting spells, the rogues loved poison and would get a bonus to poison use at the expense of health... Their second level was from either barbarian, cleric, druid, fighter, ranger, rogue, or sorcerer. Add to that an assortment of equipment and the party was underway fairly quickly.

Outcome

I made the mistake of allowing the players three goblins each. The NPCS were generally level 3-7 and were in groups of 4-8. Having 12 level 2 characters who acted in malicious unison was devastating. The patrols were a joke and served only to increase the party's blood lust.

After scouting a few caves the players decided to attack a cave bear and used the terrain to annihilate the poor beast. The following raids by orc hunters met a similar fate though some damage was taken by the party.

We haven't had a chance to finish the campaign yet.

For example: What are some common mistakes when first living in,building, or moving your tiny house? Anything you wish you would have known earlier? Advice for first timers?
What are the do's and don'ts of living in, or building a tiny house? Advice for first timers?

So, I'm not the best person to be commenting here since I have never built a tiny house, and haven't lived in one since I was a child. I do however remember living in one as a kid. My biggest one is simply storage... you need so much less stuff than you think you do, and a tiny house will show you how true that is. The other thing is a combination of built in shelving (recessed bookshelves in the wall) and multi-use. That's more of a lesson from living on a boat a fair bit as a kid - you can arrange a space so that your kitchen table becomes a bed for example. Things like that become not just practical, but require, when you are living in a tiny space.
This is true. Thanks for your input.

Moved from a 1500 sq ft apartment to a 500 sq ft cabin. What we did was to measure all existing furniture/large electronics, and give away/sell what would be too large. On the paper layout plan, we tried to fit to scale what was left, and what we felt was going to overcrowd the room, we got rid off.

We got new beds that have in built storage, thats a big plus. We keep switching winter/summer clothing and stuff that doesn't need to come out often there. Reducing stuff you don't need feels great actually!
